extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century philosophical exposition comparing utilitarian, intuitive, and aesthetic accounts of moral judgment, conscience, and the hierarchy of pleasures and virtues. The text aims to classify moral feelings, explain their origins, and evaluate competing theories of moral obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarian criterion (actions judged by happiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The utilitarian rule of judging actions and dispositions by their tendency to promote or diminish happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a clear standard but criticised: utilitarianism allegedly explains conscience as 'casual and artificial association' and, if carried to logical conclusions, would be 'subversive of morality' because the more the mind analyses the origin of the moral motive the more its influence must decline. Examples/arguments: pleasures of the senses have a real foundation; pleasures of virtue, per utilitarians, rest on habit and association and so lack coercive moral weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian universalizability as a guide
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim of Kant that man should always act so that the rule of his conduct might be adopted as a law by all rational beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledged as useful as a practical guide, but the text argues that for it to carry moral weight it 'is necessary to presuppose the sense of moral obligation'—i.e., the Kantian formulation needs the underlying conscience or sense of duty to function as binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of moral obligation / conscience as distinct faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience involves 'the sense of obligation and of legitimate supremacy' which is 'the essential and characteristic feature of conscience' and distinguishes it from all other parts of our nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argued to be generically distinct from pleasure/pain or mere association; conscience supplies an imperative character to conduct and cannot be reduced to feelings of pleasure or to habit. Examples: lawful government appropriating land vs colonists murdering savages—one act feels innocent, the other wrong even if both are done with impunity; conscience judges independently of rewards/punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral judgments include an intellectual element distinct from liking/disliking
rubrics_metrics.description: At the root of morals lies 'an intellectual judgment which is clearly distinct from liking or disliking, from pleasure or from pain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by cases where self-reproach occurs without moral culpability (foolish but innocent acts)—we still distinguish moral reprobation from other grounds of shame. Thus moral evaluation is not reducible to mere emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience can be a source of more pain than pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience's reproaches are often more felt than its approval, and considered apart from the course of action it prescribes, conscience may cause more pain than pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes the rarity of self-complacency among virtuous people and that moral growth often increases sensitiveness of conscience, checked by modesty and humility; this bears on the motivational role and psychological costs of conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure disinterestedness as the root of true virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of pure disinterestedness is presupposed in our estimates of virtue and is 'the root of all the emotions with which we contemplate acts of heroism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue is described as pursuing what one believes right even at cost of pain, disaster, or early death and without prospect of reward—this distinguishes moral action from selfish calculation or habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive case for a moral faculty (method of discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who maintain a moral faculty 'arrive at it by a process of induction'—they examine, analyse, classify moral feelings and only assign them to a special faculty when incapable of resolution into other elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that asserting a moral faculty is not dogmatic: it is the result of observation and analysis of moral sentiments through their formation stages; observation's function is to 'follow them through all the stages of their formation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation/classification of faculties (moral, æsthetic, appetites)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'faculty' is an expression of classification: moral faculty differs from æsthetic faculty; conscience surveys the whole constitution of our being and can judge and restrain appetites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that distinguishing faculties does not imply physical organs; it denotes different trains of mental phenomena. Conscience's uniqueness is emphasized—it is superior to and can restrain other appetites and tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy and limits between moral and æsthetical judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a close connection between the good and the beautiful: aesthetic judgments include intuition and emotion similar to moral judgments, and both can be immediate and universal in broad features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But limits exist: terms like 'beautiful' fit virtues like charity or devotion but less well apply to duties of perfect obligation (veracity, integrity). Also conscience has a unique, regulatory role that separates morals from merely æsthetical appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilisation as a modifier of moral and æsthetic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and æsthetical judgments vary with degrees of civilisation; the moral standard changes within limits according to society's evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: virtues prized in rude civilisations (discipline, courage) may be less valued in organised societies; preferences in taste shift (gaudy vs chaste styles); national circumstances and environment shape standards (e.g., views of beauty across peoples). Accidental causes and influential figures can also vitiate natural taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher and lower pleasures / higher vs lower faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference of kind among pleasures and faculties—some pleasures (mental, æsthetical) are of a 'higher order' than bodily pleasures (e.g., palate), and this is not reducible to intensity or duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and contrasts: music vs taste; tragedy vs farce; beauty vs grotesque—cultivation elevates certain pleasures and creates fastidiousness, and civilisation tends toward higher pleasures even if total realised enjoyment is not greater. The superiority of mental pleasures informs moral valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of accidental causes and social imitation in forming standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Many diversities in moral and æsthetical judgments trace to accidental causes: influential persons, peculiar customs, or religious systems can elevate indifferent actions to honour or vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such local or accidental standards may require appeal to a wider tribunal to correct error; national types and fashions can distort taste and moral assessment (examples: English footman's contempt for French uniforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation's role vs purely deductive explanation in moral philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of observation is not merely to attest moral sentiments but 'to follow them through all the stages of their formation' rather than to settle for a deductive explanation alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques the simplistic reading of 'inductive' moralists; both proponents and opponents of a moral faculty use induction—what differs is whether observed moral phenomena are resolved into other causes or assigned to a distinct faculty.
